title: Node rotation and failure recovery — bare metal & vSphere
content:
Purpose:
This runbook covers safe node rotation and failure recovery workflows for on‑prem Kubernetes clusters managed across bare metal (IPMI/iPXE) and vSphere environments. It focuses on a minimal‑blast radius approach for worker and optional control-plane replacements, Terraform module notes for reprovisioning, and an incremental upgrade/rollback plan for tokenized kubeadm joins.

Scope & audience:
- Audience: platform engineers and SREs running Private deployments.
- Scope: worker node replacement, emergency replacement for failed control plane node (if HA not present), rejoin procedures, Terraform-driven reprovision, and verification tests.
- Not covered: full cluster restore from backup, major Kubernetes version upgrades (see separate upgrade playbook).

Assumptions & prerequisites:
- You have cluster-admin credentials (kubectl context) and access to the private deployment vault for secrets (bmc/ipmi creds, vSphere service account, bootstrap tokens).
- Terraform state is stored remotely (S3-compatible or Terraform Cloud) and you can run apply against the infra modules.
- Standard kubeadm bootstrap flow is used for control-plane joins. If the cluster uses a different bootstrap system, adapt the join steps accordingly.
- Images/templates are prepared and stored in an image registry or vSphere template library.

Inventory & quick checks (preflight):
- Identify failed node: kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep NotReady
- Confirm pods on node: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>
- Check cloud/vSphere/BMC: ping IP, ssh (if present), BMC console for hardware diagnostics or vSphere VM power state.
- Check Terraform drift: terraform plan on the node module (dry run) to see if instance count or config differs.

High-level decision flow:
1) Is the node recoverable in-place? If yes, prefer repair.
2) If unrecoverable or uncertain, replace the node (create new instance, drain old metadata, remove old from inventory).
3) For control-plane failures: if single control-plane and broken, coordinate forensic snapshot and consider restore from backup/standby (see control-plane emergency section).

Worker node replacement — detailed steps (bare metal):
- Mark node unschedulable and drain:
  kubectl cordon <node>
  kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force
- Note daemonset behavior: check whether local‑storage pods need special handling.
- Remove node from cluster (optional prior to reprovision): kubectl delete node <node>
- Reprovision via IPMI/iPXE/ignition:
  - Option A: reprovision using our terraform module (tf-module-baremetal-node). Change instance metadata (replace mac/serial mapping) and run terraform apply.
  - Option B: manual IPMI PXE boot cycle: use ipmitool chassis power cycle and ensure the node loads the correct iPXE script.
- Terraform notes (bare metal):
  - Module: modules/baremetal/node
  - Inputs to set for new node: hostname, mac_address, bmc_ip (or bmc_id), image_profile, provisioning_tags
  - Secrets: bmc_creds are fetched from vault provider (do not hardcode in tfvars)
  - Replace flow: keep node count stable; create a new node resource first and then decommission the old one to avoid capacity drops. Example sequence: set desired_count +=1, terraform apply -> wait for new node Ready -> cordon & drain old node -> remove old node resource -> terraform apply to decrement.
- Once the new machine boots, run join: kubeadm join <control-plane-ip>:6443 --token <token> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash>
  - Retrieve token: kubeadm token create --print-join-command (run on control plane)
  - Ensure kubelet service is enabled and CRI socket path matches cluster setup (containerd vs docker).
- Verify: kubectl get nodes; check Prometheus node exporter, kubelet metrics; confirm application pods scheduled as expected.

Worker node replacement — vSphere flow:
- Drain node (same as bare metal).
- Use vSphere template or VM cloning pipeline: our terraform module (tf-module-vsphere-node) expects inputs: template_name, datastore, resource_pool, network_profiles, customization_spec.
- Best practice: use linked clones with updated cloud-init that contains a bootstrap script to run kubeadm join from Vault-provisioned token.
- Terraform sequence: create new VM resource with unique name and tag; wait for VMware tools/guest ready; ensure guest customization script executed and kubelet registers.
- Remove old VM from inventory after verification.

Control-plane emergency replacement (single-control-plane):
- If PD control plane node is NotReady and cannot be recovered quickly:
  1) Snapshot etcd (if accessible) or copy /etc/kubernetes/pki and /var/lib/etcd to safe store.
  2) Stand up a temporary control plane on an existing worker or new VM using kubeadm init --config with recovered certs OR use kubeadm restore flow.
  3) Rejoin remaining control-plane members once etcd is healthy.
- If cluster is multi-master with quorum lost, follow the multi‑master recovery doc (link at top). This runbook only includes minimal emergency steps.

Rolling replace for OS/kernel/security patching (planned maintenance):
- Readiness window: ensure HPA/minReplicas are configured and disruption budgets exist for critical apps.
- Plan: drain one node at a time, validate pod rescheduling, run local sanity checks (smoke tests), and move to next node.
- If using Terraform-managed node pools, prefer the in-place increase/replace pattern described in bare metal notes to avoid accidental whole-pool replacement.

Rollback plan (if new nodes fail to join or apps break):
- If a newly provisioned node fails to join: power down and destroy the VM/hardware resource; reattempt with previous template or base image.
- If deployment of a new kubelet config causes issues: revert kubelet config via automation run (Ansible/ssh) to previous known-good config and restart kubelet.
- If too many pods drain failure: re-enable scheduling on previous nodes and scale app back down to stable state.

Verification checklist after rotation:
- kubectl get nodes (all Ready)
- kubectl get cs (componentstatuses) ok (or use control-plane endpoints health checks)
- All DaemonSets running everywhere: kubectl get daemonsets --all-namespaces -o wide
- No CrashLoopBackOffs: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces | grep CrashLoopBackOff
- Metrics: node exporter and kubelet metrics flowing to Prometheus; check alert suppression for maintenance alerts.

Common failure modes and quick diagnostics:
- kubelet not registering: check /var/log/kubelet.log and journalctl -u kubelet. Common causes: wrong CRI socket, hostname mismatch, stale kubelet.conf CA.
- token expired for kubeadm join: generate a new join token on a healthy control plane: kubeadm token create --print-join-command
- network plugin flaps: verify CNI agent logs (calico/rook/flannel) and network policies. If CNI fails, pods may not start even when node Ready.
- BMC unreachable: verify network/VLAN to BMC, use dedicated OOB network, escalate to on-site engineering if hardware console access required.

Operational tooling tips & Terraform module design notes:
- Module naming: tf-module-baremetal-node, tf-module-vsphere-node. Keep a small surface area of inputs; secrets via Vault provider only.
- Idempotency: modules should try to be idempotent with predictable resource names. Use lifecycle.ignore_changes for metadata fields that change outside Terraform (e.g., tags applied by provisioning pipeline).
- Replacement pattern: implement an explicit desired_count field plus an "evict_node" variable to allow orchestrated increase-then-decrease flows. Example var set: { desired_count = 6, evict_node = "worker-03" } where apply creates a worker-07 then terraform apply again removes worker-03.
- Join automation: embed a small bootstrap agent in images that pulls join commands securely from Vault and retries with backoff. Avoid hardcoding join tokens in images.

Postmortem & tagging convention:
- Tag replaced nodes with tags: replaced_by=<ticket>, replaced_at=<date> in inventory. Keep a small audit file in /var/lib/platform/replacements.log for future forensic.

Quick commands cheat sheet:
- Drain: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
- Cordon: kubectl cordon <node>
- Delete node: kubectl delete node <node>
- Create join token on control plane: kubeadm token create --print-join-command
- Check kubelet logs: sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 --no-pager

Notes & open questions:
- Should we add an automated, circuit‑breaker policy to the provisioning pipeline that halts a rolling replace if >20% of nodes are failing join within 30 minutes? (proposal: yes — ticket JIRA-OPS-1502)
- Consider a tamperproof ledger (S3 write-only) for node replacement audit entries.

Appendix: sample terraform snippet (illustrative)

# Example (tfvars style)
# node_pool.us-west-1.tfvars
# desired_count = 6
# evict_node = "worker-03"
# image_profile = "ubuntu-22-04-k8s-bootstrap-2026-01"

# Example module call (pseudo-terraform)
# module "worker_pool" {
#   source = "git::ssh://git.redwood.internal/infra/terraform-modules//baremetal/node"
#   desired_count = var.desired_count
#   image_profile = var.image_profile
#   vault_role = var.vault_role
# }

End of runbook.
